answer.sourceLine: These really are Emerson’s words, from a letter to one of his daughters away at school — printed in his authorised biographer James Elliot Cabot’s A Memoir of Ralph Waldo Emerson, vol. II (Riverside Press, 1887), chapter XIII, p. 489, where the passage is confirmed verbatim in the scanned first edition. Quote Investigator dates the manuscript letter to 8 April 1854 and names the recipient as his daughter Ellen; note that the wording everyone shares is a condensation, with one sentence dropped from the middle.

source.excerpt: To one of his daughters who was away from home, at school, he writes: — “Finish every day and be done with it. For manners and for wise living it is a vice to remember. You have done what you could; some blunders and absurdities no doubt crept in; forget them as soon as you can. To-morrow is a new day; you shall begin it well and serenely, and with too high a spirit to be cumbered with your old nonsense. This day for all that is good and fair. It is too dear, with its hopes and invitations, to waste a moment on the rotten yesterdays.”
trail: 8 April 1854 — Emerson writes to his daughter Ellen, away at school. Quote Investigator ↗ gives that date and recipient, and transcribes the rough manuscript wording from the Columbia University Press six-volume collection of the letters (1939), vol. 4, pp. 438–439: “You must finish a term & finish every day, & be done with it.”

1887 — James Elliot Cabot, Emerson’s literary executor and family-approved biographer, prints a smoothed and fully punctuated version in A Memoir of Ralph Waldo Emerson, vol. II ↗, chapter XIII, p. 489, introducing it only as a letter “to one of his daughters who was away from home, at school.” This is the text later anthologies copy.

1943–1982 — anthologists trim and reshape it. The Thesaurus of Epigrams (1943) prints the shortened three-sentence form that circulates today, and Dale Carnegie’s Scrapbook (1959) changes the opening to “Finish each day” — the variant chain is laid out by Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — the passage is absent from Wikiquote’s Emerson page ↗ in every section, sourced and disputed alike, so the provenance runs through Cabot and Rusk rather than the usual quote listings.
source.excerptNote: Cabot prints the letter without naming the daughter or giving a date. The widely quoted form drops the second sentence, “For manners and for wise living it is a vice to remember,” and turns the semicolon after “could” into a full stop.

source.rightsNote: The wording shown here follows James Elliot Cabot’s A Memoir of Ralph Waldo Emerson, published in 1887 and long in the public domain in the United States; Emerson himself died in 1882 and wrote the letter in 1854. The rougher manuscript wording quoted in the trail comes from Ralph L. Rusk’s 1939 edition of the letters, a later edited work — the sentences on this page are the 1887 text.

author.bio: Emerson (born 25 May 1803, died 27 April 1882) was an American essayist, lecturer, poet and former minister who led the Transcendentalist movement, formulating its philosophy in his 1836 essay Nature. Much of his living came from the lecture circuit, and his biographer placed this letter in a chapter on his ways with his children — where Emerson is shown teaching them, from the age of “thirteen or fourteen,” the whole of his own doctrine of self-reliance. He had four children: Waldo, Ellen, Edith and Edward.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is right — Emerson really wrote it. What has drifted is the wording, and the fact that almost nobody can say where it comes from.

items.why: The trimmed version in circulation drops Cabot’s second sentence, “For manners and for wise living it is a vice to remember,” and turns the semicolon after “you could” into a full stop. Quote Investigator ↗ traces that exact trimmed form to the 1943 Thesaurus of Epigrams.

items.who: “Finish each day and be done with it”
items.why: A widely circulated version swaps “every” for “each.” Quote Investigator ↗ finds that change in Dale Carnegie’s Scrapbook (1959) and again in Leonard Safir and William Safire’s Good Advice (1982). The 1887 text reads “every.”

items.who: Quoted with no source at all
items.why: Cabot printed the letter in 1887 without naming the recipient or giving a date, and the passage does not appear on Wikiquote’s Emerson page ↗ in any section — so the usual online copies cite nothing checkable. The date and the daughter’s name come from Quote Investigator ↗, working from Rusk’s 1939 edition of the letters.

misattribution.truthLine: Emerson wrote it, in a letter to his daughter Ellen dated 8 April 1854 by Quote Investigator ↗; the familiar wording is James Elliot Cabot’s 1887 tidy-up of the manuscript, verifiable at page 489 of volume II of his Memoir ↗, later trimmed by anthologists.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cabot sets this letter inside a chapter on Emerson’s ways with his children, as evidence that from “thirteen or fourteen” he did not hesitate to inculcate in them the whole of his own doctrine of self-reliance. The advice itself is not lofty at all: stop replaying the day’s embarrassments, because dwelling on them is a bad habit rather than a virtue.

That is also why the sentence anthologists keep cutting is the one worth keeping. “For manners and for wise living it is a vice to remember” is the actual argument; the rest is the consolation. Lose it and a father’s reasoning becomes a fridge magnet.
detailsBody: Emerson dashed the letter off with ampersands and almost no punctuation. Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the manuscript text from the Columbia University Press six-volume collection of Emerson’s letters (1939), vol. 4, pp. 438–439, and it opens quite differently: “You must finish a term & finish every day, & be done with it.”

Cabot, who was Emerson’s literary executor and family-approved biographer, printed a tidied version in 1887 — adding the semicolons and full stops that make the passage quotable. The anthology versions Quote Investigator traces all descend from Cabot, not the manuscript.

One small provenance oddity: Cabot placed the letter in a chapter he opens by describing “the period from 1835 to 1845,” even though the letter dates from 1854. He grouped it by theme rather than by date, and gave neither the date nor the daughter’s name — which is why the citation trail had to wait for Rusk.

schema.claimReviewed: Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote the lines quoted as “Finish every day and be done with it. You have done what you could. Some blunders and absurdities no doubt crept in; forget them as soon as you can” — in a letter of 8 April 1854 to his daughter Ellen. The attribution is verified; the circulating wording is a later condensation of the passage James Elliot Cabot printed in 1887, which also carries the sentence “For manners and for wise living it is a vice to remember.”
